lesson.title: Three Parts, One Building Block: Inside the Nucleotide
lesson.summary: A nucleotide is a three-part molecule built from a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar, and a nitrogenous base, and while chains of nucleotides form DNA and RNA, individual nucleotides also work on their own as energy carriers and signaling molecules.
lesson.body:
Every nucleotide is built from three connected pieces: a five-carbon sugar at the center, a phosphate group attached to one side of that sugar, and a nitrogenous base attached to the other side. The sugar is a pentose, a five-carbon monosaccharide, and which pentose is present is exactly what distinguishes the two kinds of nucleic acid: DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose, while RNA nucleotides contain ribose. The only chemical difference between them is small but important, ribose has a hydroxyl group on its second carbon, while deoxyribose has only a hydrogen atom there instead, which is why it is called deoxy, meaning missing an oxygen.

The nitrogenous base attached to the sugar comes in two structural families. Purines, adenine and guanine, are built from two fused rings, while pyrimidines, cytosine, thymine, and uracil, are built from a single ring. Thymine appears only in DNA, uracil appears only in RNA, and adenine, guanine, and cytosine appear in both. These bases are rich in nitrogen containing functional groups, amine groups in particular, arranged around each ring in specific patterns, and it is these functional groups that will later allow bases to form precise hydrogen bonds with their partner base, a topic covered in DNA and RNA structure.

There is a useful distinction between a nucleoside and a nucleotide. A nucleoside is just the sugar bonded to a base, with no phosphate attached at all, while a nucleotide is a nucleoside with one or more phosphate groups attached. In fact, the molecules cells actually use to build new DNA or RNA strands are nucleoside triphosphates, carrying three linked phosphate groups rather than one. When a new nucleotide is added to a growing nucleic acid chain, two of those three phosphates are cleaved off, and the energy released by breaking those high energy phosphate bonds is what powers the condensation reaction that forms the new phosphodiester bond.

Nucleotides are not only used to build nucleic acid polymers, several of them have important jobs entirely on their own. Adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, is chemically just the nucleotide adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups, but instead of being incorporated into RNA, it usually functions independently as the cell's main short-term energy currency, its terminal phosphate bond releasing usable energy when broken. Other nucleotide-based molecules, such as NAD+, act as electron carriers in cellular metabolism, showing that the basic nucleotide structure has been repurposed by cells for jobs well beyond information storage.

It is only when many nucleotides are linked together, one phosphodiester bond at a time through the condensation reactions described in nucleic acids, that the true information carrying polymers of the cell take shape. Those two polymers, built from deoxyribonucleotides and ribonucleotides respectively, are DNA and RNA, and their distinct three-dimensional structures are examined next.
